rationale: The new hazardous solvent introduces a chemical hazard that employees have not previously been trained about; effective hazard communication training is required when it is introduced. The training must cover the specified detection, hazard, protective-measure, program/label, and SDS topics. Because the employer uses the hazardous solvent, it must have its safety data sheet in the workplace. The portable-container labeling exception cannot be applied because the facts do not establish that the containers are intended only for the immediate use of the employee performing the transfer.

The technician is an employee who is newly assigned to operate a process covered by §1910.119. Before being involved in operating that newly assigned process, the employer must train the employee in an overview of the process and in the operating procedures specified in §1910.119(f). The stated start date next week makes this a pre-assignment training obligation. The relevant evidence is a record showing completion of that required training.

Because this is a covered PSM process and the equipment/technology modification is not a replacement in kind, written management-of-change procedures apply. The modification changes process safety information, so that information must be updated. Because the modification is significant enough to require a process-safety-information change, a pre-startup safety review is required before restart. Before highly hazardous chemicals are introduced, that review must confirm conformance with design specifications, adequate safety/operating/maintenance/emergency procedures, completion of management of change for the modified facility, and completed training for each employee operating the process. Operating procedures must also be reviewed as necessary to reflect the chemical, technology, equipment, and facility changes.

The near miss occurred at a covered process and could reasonably have resulted in a catastrophic toxic release. Therefore, the employer must investigate the incident under §1910.119(m)(1). No employee injury, hospitalization, fatality, amputation, or loss of an eye is stated, so the supplied record does not support selecting an OSHA fatality/severe-injury reporting requirement.

Because the recordkeeping-covered establishment had 300 employees during the year covered, it must create and certify the OSHA 300A annual summary, post it conspicuously by February 1 through April 30 without alteration or coverage, electronically submit Form 300A information to OSHA or its designee, and retain the required records for five years following the covered calendar year. The supplied §1904.41(a)(1)(ii) excerpt establishes the electronic-submission duty but does not provide a submission date.

The approaching anniversary triggers the required periodic inspection. The supplied scenario establishes that employees service equipment subject to the hazardous-energy condition described in the standard, and the cited requirement requires an inspection of the energy control procedure at least annually to verify that both the procedure and the standard are being followed. An inspection record is the pertinent evidence.

The stated activity is covered servicing, and the described unexpected startup and stored pneumatic-energy release could cause injury. Therefore, the machine must be isolated and rendered inoperative under an established energy-control program; documented, specific energy-control procedures must be used; required isolating devices must isolate the machine from its energy sources; and stored or residual pneumatic energy must be relieved, disconnected, restrained, or otherwise rendered safe. The program also requires at least annual periodic inspection of the energy-control procedure. The supplied facts do not indicate a job, machine/process, or procedure change, so retraining-on-change is not selected.

Because the contractor is being selected to work in a covered PSM process area, the employer must obtain and evaluate the contract employer's safety performance and programs. Before the work, the employer must inform the contract employer of known potential fire, explosion, or toxic-release hazards related to the work and process. The contract employer must assure that each contract employee is instructed on those known hazards and applicable emergency action plan provisions. The stated facts support these contractor-management requirements without requiring a hot-work, incident-log, change-management, or OSHA-recordkeeping determination.

The requester is a former employee seeking the OSHA 301 Incident Report describing that former employee's own injury, and the employer maintains the requested report. The employer must provide a copy containing that information by the end of the next business day.

An authorized employee representative has requested OSHA 301 Incident Reports for an establishment where the representative represents employees under a collective bargaining agreement. The employer must provide copies within 7 calendar days, limited to the OSHA 301 section titled "Tell us about the case," with all other information removed.

Because an employee died as a result of a work-related incident, the employer must report the fatality to OSHA within eight hours. The supplied excerpt for general recordkeeping does not establish that the fatality meets a stated general recording criterion, so it is not selected.

Each employer required by this part to keep records of fatalities, injuries, and illnesses must record each fatality, injury and illness that is work-related; is a new case; and meets one or more of the general recording criteria.
rationale: The work-related incident involved both an in-patient hospitalization and an amputation, each of which triggers OSHA reporting within 24 hours under the supplied excerpt. The organization states that the case is recordable, supporting recording of the work-related injury.

The employer must maintain a reasonable injury-reporting procedure that does not deter or discourage accurate reporting. It also must not discharge or discriminate against an employee for reporting a work-related injury or illness. The supervisor's threatened discipline following a report is relevant evidence that the reporting process may be deterrent and that prohibited discrimination may have occurred. The supplied facts do not establish that the injury is recordable or reportable to OSHA.

Because the covered PSM process's compliance audit identified deficiencies, the employer must promptly determine and document an appropriate response to each audit finding and document that the deficiencies have been corrected.

The scheduled inspection of covered-process equipment supports the inspection-and-test documentation requirement in §1910.119(j)(4). Because the vessel was found outside acceptable limits, §1910.119(j)(5) requires correction before further use, or correction in a safe and timely manner when necessary means are taken to assure safe operation. Determining whether the vessel may continue to be used and what corrective measures adequately assure safe operation requires qualified engineering and safety judgment.
missing_information_or_escalation_reason: Qualified engineering/safety evaluation is needed to determine the applicable process-safety-information limits, the deficiency’s severity, whether continued operation can be made safe, and the corrective-action timeframe and controls.

rationale: The employer uses the hazardous chemical in the employee's work area, so it must have an SDS in the workplace for that chemical. It also must ensure that the SDS is readily accessible during every work shift to employees in their work areas. The stated inability to immediately access the SDS during the night shift indicates that the immediate-access requirement is not met.

The portable container is filled from a labeled hazardous-chemical drum, is intended only for the immediate use of the employee performing the transfer, remains under that employee's control, and is not stored for later use. Therefore, the portable-container labeling exception applies and the employer is not required to label that portable container.

rationale: The supplied OSHA LOTO excerpt directly requires that the employee who applied the lockout or tagout device remove it. Because that employee has left and cannot be reached, the supplied context does not support management directing another employee to remove the device.

Because one employer's hazardous chemicals may expose employees of another employer at the shared worksite, each employer that produces, uses, or stores those chemicals must ensure its written hazard communication program includes methods to provide the other on-site employer access to safety data sheets for each hazardous chemical.

These facts create a substantive dispute over whether it is a replacement in kind or an equipment change subject to the employer's written management-of-change procedures. The supplied excerpt expressly excludes only replacements in kind, but does not define technical equivalence or resolve the engineering disagreement.
missing_information_or_escalation_reason: Qualified engineering and process-safety review is needed to determine whether the changed material specification and operating limit are technically equivalent to the existing component, or instead constitute an equipment change requiring management of change. The record should establish the applicable design specifications, process safety information, operating envelope, and basis for the replacement-in-kind determination.

rationale: A 24-hour OSHA report is required only when an employee's in-patient hospitalization results from a work-related incident. The supplied facts establish that the employee was admitted to a hospital after becoming ill, but do not establish either predicate.
missing_information_or_escalation_reason: Determine whether the illness resulted from a work-related incident and whether the hospital admission was an in-patient hospitalization.

rationale: Federal OSHA requires effective information and training when a new chemical hazard that employees have not previously been trained about is introduced into their work area. Ordering a cleaning product can trigger this evaluation, but the supplied facts do not establish that the product is hazardous or that it introduces a hazard not already covered by employee training.
missing_information_or_escalation_reason: Obtain the product safety data sheet or other hazard classification information and determine whether the product will be introduced into employees' work area. Also compare its hazards with the hazards addressed in applicable employee training records.

rationale: Outside servicing personnel must mutually inform the on-site and outside employers of their respective lockout/tagout procedures only when they will perform activities covered by the scope and application of the lockout/tagout standard. Covered servicing or maintenance exists where unexpected energization, startup, or release of stored energy could occur and cause injury. The scenario confirms outside-vendor routine maintenance but does not establish that hazard predicate.
missing_information_or_escalation_reason: Determine whether the maintenance exposes employees to a potential unexpected energization, startup, or release of stored/residual energy that could cause injury. If yes, the work is covered and the on-site and outside employers must inform each other of their respective lockout/tagout procedures.
